P	Use this procedure when you need an artifact, but none of the existing options fit. Or, use it when you have an idea that you want to flesh out. As you work through each step, take notes on your decisions or results.

H3	2a. Mundane
P	It's no magical wonder, but it's still interesting, useful, and/or valuable. Pick or roll for why they might care.
P	1d12 why they might care
P	1 It'd make a good trophy/gift/thing to show the kids (Value 0)
P	2 It's useful—like a tool, a weapon, supplies, etc. (Value 0 or 1)
P	3 It's useful but also unusual, specialized, uncommon (Value 1)
P	4 It's fine, beautiful, excellent (Value 1)
P	5 It's of a distinct origin/style (Value
P	1 or 2 to a collector)
P	6 It's inherently valuable—silver, trade goods, etc. (Value 2)
P	7 It's a true luxury and/or a symbol of status (Value 2)
P	8 It's precious, but only to the right buyer (Value 2 or 3)
P	9 It's exquisitely made, a thing of beauty (Value 3)
P	10 It's inherently valuable—gold, gems, exotic goods, etc. (Value 3)
P	11 It's a clue, or it hints at the bigger picture, and roll 1d10 again
P	12 It presents an opportunity: a key, a resource they might mine, a map, etc.
P	Now, go pick or roll for its <b>form</b> (page 505, step 3).

HR

P	7 Fills those who look upon it with ___ (greed, rage, peace, joy, etc.)

P	10 Glows/thrums/vibrates in the presence of ___ (gold, magic, lies, poison, etc.)
P	11 Protects against/repels ___ (emotional magic, fire/heat, ghosts, etc.)
P	12 Roll twice, but treat one of the results as a drawback or flaw

P	Pick or roll for the nature of this binding.

HR

P	8-9 Trapped by accident, desperation, twist of fate
P	10-12 Dwells here naturally, spontaneously Then, pick a spirit or sentience appropriate to the binding, origin, and theme. If you're unsure, roll 1d12.

H3	2g. Magical effect
P	Pick or roll for the magic's function (what it does) as well as its drawback. Combine them with its origin and theme to imagine what spell, power, blessing, or curse is involved.
P	1d12 function
HR
P	1 Create/conjure/craft
P	2 Defend/repel/secure
P	3 Destroy/slay/consume
P	4 Contain/bind/capture
P	5 Enhance/refine/purify
P	6 Reduce/diminish/suppress
P	7 Sustain/heal/repair
P	8 Sense/identify/reveal
P	9 Hide/disguise/confuse
P	10 Manipulate/control/compel
P	11 Transform/combine/reshape
P	12 Roll twice and combine
P	1d12 drawback
HR
P	1 Scarring: leaves a lasting thematic mark on you/the target
P	2 Dangerous: can have destructive, unwanted side effects
P	3 Demanding: takes great effort to cast/trigger/maintain
P	4 Discordant: draws unwanted attention
P	5 Fickle: fails at inopportune times
P	6 Weak: easily countered by will/ fortitude/preparation
P	7 Indiscriminate: imprecise in its targets/duration/effect
P	8 Withering: weakens you/the artifact/the target
P	9 Restricted: works only in specific, thematic conditions
P	10 Costly: requires sacrifice, consumes resources
P	11 Slow: takes time to cast/manifest
P	12 Roll twice For artifacts that produce a magical effect (as opposed to spells or rituals), how often or frequently can it be used? Pick or roll.

P	1d12 usage
HR
P	1-3 1d6 uses, then it's consumed/ruined/powerless
P	4-6 1d6 uses, then it must be recharged/ replenished
P	7-8 A few charges, which might be lost with each use; recharges with time or effort
P	9 At will, but each time is riskier/less powerful/more costly; resets with effort or slowly over time
P	10 At will, but there's a cost/risk with each use
P	11 At will, though limited by practicalities
P	12 Continuous; it's always going Now, go to step <b>3</b>, below, to pick or roll for its <b>form</b>.

P	If it's not already established or clear to you, pick or roll for the artifact's size.
P	<b>1d12</b> size
HR
P	1-2 A small item
P	3-4 A item or object ◇
P	5-6 A ◇◇ item or object
P	7-8 An <i>immobile</i> object or place
P	9-10 Roll 1d8 again, but it's hard to extract, access, and/or take advantage of
P	11-12 Roll 1d10 again, but it's also <i>crude</i>, <i>fragile</i>, <i>cumbersome</i>, and/or <i>dangerous</i> Now, what is it, exactly? Pick or roll.
P	Interpret the results liberally, keeping in mind the origin, theme, and other details about the item. Let yourself be inspired!
P	Note: an artifact might very well be made from or with an appropriate <b>strange</b> <b>material</b> (page 500, step 2b), even if you didn't get that result. Maybe your Forge Lord sword that absorbs heat and flame is made of aetherium, or has a red crystal for its pommel.
P	1d12 what is it?
HR
P	1-8 Something more common (next page)
P	9-12 Something less common (next page)

P	1d12 more common

P	1 Agriculture: seed, spade, flail, hoe, fork, scythe, plow, millstone, etc.
P	2 Construction: nail, brick, tile, trowel, timber, masonry, wall, etc.
P	3 Container: lock/key, pouch, box, urn, chest, cell, vault, etc.
P	4 Domestic: utensil, spindle, vessel, broom, foodstuffs, crib, loom, etc.
P	5 Fire: incense, oil, candle, lamp, lantern, sconce, brazier, hearth, etc.
P	6 Liquid: oil, spirits, vial, wineskin, cup, jug, barrel, fount, bath, etc.
P	7 Protection: talisman, helm, cloak, armor, shield, door, wall, etc.
P	8 Remains: ashes, scale, fang, horn, organ, bone, hide, skeleton, etc.
P	9 Textile: fibers, scarf, footwear, rope, clothes, furs, bedding, tapestry, etc.
P	10 Tool: needle, file, chisel, saw, mallet, shovel, anvil, workspace, etc.
P	11 Trade: coin, coins, satchel, scales, wheel, sled, cart, wagon, etc.
P	12 Violence: knife, poison, sword, rod, staff, bow, spear, banner, etc.
P	For example, if you started with "a ◇◇ item or object" and then got a 4 on the table above, that could be a quern stone or a small cauldron. But "an <i>immobile</i> object or place" plus a roll of 8 above might a mammoth tusk, or a whole ossuary!
P	1d12 less common
P	1 Art: pigments, brushes, carving, figurine, chisel, painting, statuary, etc.
P	2 Beauty: cosmetics, jewelry, comb, torc, circlet, mirror, robes, regalia, etc.
P	3 Curiosity: wonder, device, enigma, doohickey, toy, etc.
P	4 Husbandry: collar, brush, prod, bridle, saddle, harness, stable, etc.
P	5 Raw material: powder, salt, chemics, grains, ingot, ore, slab, timber, etc.
P	6 Music: notation, bell, chime, flute, rattle, horn, lyre, lute, drum, etc.
P	7 Natural: flower, feather, shell, rock, wood, tree, spring, cave, etc.
P	8 Prosthesis: eye, teeth, hand, foot, arm, leg, crutch, wheelchair, etc.
P	9 Religion: symbol, offering, idol, altar, ceremonial ___ (roll again)
P	10 Specialized equipment: astrolabe, level, gear, decanter, still, kiln, etc.
P	11 Writing: ink, runes, stylus, scroll, parchment, tablet, codex, archive, etc.
P	12 Highly decorated and/or exquisitely made more common object (previous column)
P	Note: an artifact might very well be made from or with an appropriate <b>strange</b> <b>material</b> (page 500, step 2b), even if you didn't get that result. Maybe your Forge Lord sword that absorbs heat and flame is made of aetherium, or has a red crystal for its pommel.
P	For example, if you started with "a small item" and rolled a 10 on this table, you might see "decanter" and think of a little vial of perfume or maybe poison. And maybe it's the liquid that's special, not the container!
PAGE	507
HR
H2	4	Synthesis
P	Consider the details you've established. Imagine the artifact that they suggest. Fill in any missing details and start making final decisions. What is this artifact, exactly? What was it originally for?
P	How did it come to be, or be <i>here</i>?
P	You don't need a full history of the item. But try to picture something that makes sense, something that at least hints at a story.
P	As you make these decisions, it's okay to change or discard some of the details you established earlier, or to interpret them loosely or metaphorically. They're meant to spur your creativity, not to limit it.
HR
H2	5	Write-up
P	Once you've got a clear picture in your mind, write up the artifact as one of the following:
B	A <b>brief description</b> and some tags, like ~20 words or fewer
B	A <b>detailed description</b>, with a title, some tags, and a few sentences about what it is, what it looks like, what it does (if anything), what it involves
B	A brief or detailed description (as above), plus one or more <b>custom player</b> <b>moves</b>, each with a trigger, results, and maybe a roll
B	A <b>steading improvement</b>, something that, with time and effort, can provide lasting benefit to the village.
B	A <b>minor arcanum</b>, a little card you give the player with a description and requirements on the front, and the benefits of meeting them on the back.
B	A <b>major arcanum</b>: a half-page playbook insert, with unlockable moves/options and consequences for using them.
P	Keep in mind who you're writing this up for. Anything you give to the players (tags, physical descriptions, custom moves, arcana) should be clear and concise. But an artifact's history, backstory, details on where it's found, the nuances of how it works… that's all for you, to inform how you introduce it and use it in play. Write out as much as you, personally, find helpful.
P	If the artifact's Value hasn't been established, consider whether it should have one and what it might be. See <i>Book I</i>, pages 92-93 for rough guidelines.
P	If you expect the artifact will be a source of trouble, also write it up as a threat (a <i>MacGuffin</i>, probably, or maybe a <i>magical</i> <i>entity</i> or even an <i>affliction</i>).
P	Refer to the artifacts throughout this book for examples. See <i>Book I</i>, page 434 for more guidance and some worked examples.
